title: JSX in Vue
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of JSX in Vue in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies JSX in Vue within Advanced Components and Rendering. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: These APIs solve specific architectural problems; they should be chosen for a concrete requirement rather than used just because they exist.

content_blocks.title: JSX in Vue: Component communication
content_blocks.alt_text: Component communication diagram for lesson 106: JSX in Vue. Parent owns the value or business intent → Child receives data and renders its view → Child emits intent; parent decides updates
content_blocks.caption: Component flow: data moves into children through props; emitted events communicate requested changes back to the owner.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Advanced Vue rendering includes dynamic and async components, KeepAlive, Teleport, provide/inject, render functions, and plugins. This lesson focuses on JSX in Vue. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: JSX fundamentals
items.text: For JSX fundamentals, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Configuring JSX support
items.text: For Configuring JSX support, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Rendering components using JSX
items.text: For Rendering components using JSX, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

items.title: JSX and template syntax trade-offs
items.text: For JSX and template syntax trade-offs, express the intended DOM result through a Vue template binding instead of directly manipulating the DOM. Keep template expressions small, use stable keys for stateful list items, and choose directives based on whether content should be created, removed, or merely hidden.

content_blocks.code:
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
const activeTab = ref('overview')
</script>
<template><button @click="activeTab = 'overview'">Overview</button><button @click="activeTab = 'activity'">Activity</button><component :is="activeTab === 'overview' ? OverviewPanel : ActivityPanel" /></template>
content_blocks.expected_output: The component type changes as activeTab changes. Supply valid imported component objects named OverviewPanel and ActivityPanel in the script.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a local Vue app after importing both components. Preserve state only when needed and consider accessible tab semantics.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through JSX in Vue with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Configuring JSX support”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Advanced Vue rendering includes dynamic and async components, KeepAlive, Teleport, provide/inject, render functions, and plugins. For JSX in Vue, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “JSX in Vue” that applies “JSX fundamentals”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “JSX fundamentals”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

summary: JSX in Vue belongs to the broader area Advanced Components and Rendering.
The main concept to practice is JSX fundamentals.
Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
